questions.question: Describe a single fixed pulley and explain what it does to a force, giving three examples of its use.
questions.expected_answer: A single fixed pulley is a grooved wheel turning on an axle in a block that is attached to something fixed, such as a beam, a flagpole top or a crane jib, with a rope running in the groove, the load on one end and the effort on the other. It changes the direction of the force: pulling down on the rope raises the load, so the user can stand on the ground and use body weight from a safe position, and several people can pull together. Examples: a well bucket, a flagpole halyard, the rope over a crane's jib to a ground-level winch, a washing line on pulleys, sash window weights, gym cable machines.

questions.question: Explain, with reference to a measurement and to the tension in the rope, why a single fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of 1.
questions.expected_answer: Hanging a 10 newton load on one end and reading a spring balance on the other while lifting slowly gives about 10 newtons, a little more because of axle friction, so load over effort is 1; pulling the rope 300 millimetres raises the load 300 millimetres. The rope is one continuous piece with the same tension throughout, the load hangs on it so the tension equals the load, and the effort pulls on the same rope so the effort equals the same tension; the pulley only turns the rope through an angle and does not divide the load between rope sections. Work in equals work out since force and distance are equal at both ends.

questions.question: Explain why a fixed pulley is still valuable despite giving no force advantage, how it combines with other devices, and what load its fixing point must carry.
questions.expected_answer: Its value is direction, position and safety: a downward pull lets the lifter use body weight and the strong leg and back muscles, stand clear of the drop or the load, and share the rope with others. It combines with winches, carrying a crane's rope from the jib down to a winch at the base so the heavy machinery sits low, and with movable pulleys in a block and tackle, where the top fixed pulley lets the final pull be downward while the lower pulleys supply the advantage. Because the rope pulls down on both sides of the wheel with the load on one and an equal effort on the other, the fixing point carries about twice the load's weight, so brackets must be rated accordingly.
